# Isaiah 10 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview of the Chapter

The chapter has two main sections: vv. 1–4 conclude the prophecy against the Northern Kingdom begun in Isaiah 9:8 (each subsection ending with the refrain "His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised"). Vv. 5–34 then address Assyria — first as God's instrument of judgment, then as the object of God's judgment for its pride, followed by promises of a preserved remnant.

**Outline (adapted from Precept Austin / Talk Thru the Bible):**
- 10:1–4: Fourth strophe against unjust rulers (concluding Isaiah 9:8–10:4)
- 10:5–19: Destruction of Assyria for its arrogance
- 10:20–34: The remnant of Israel preserved; Assyria's march and fall

---

## Verses 1–4: Woe to Unjust Rulers

**v. 1: "Woe to those who enact unjust statutes and issue oppressive decrees…"**

This verse continues the fourth "woe" strophe begun in Isaiah 9:8. The chapter break is misleading — vv. 1–4 belong with chapter 9 (Ellicott). The target is magistrates and legislators who make evil laws and record unjust decisions. The Hebrew *hoi* ("woe") is a denunciation carrying overtones of death and a funeral lament (Precept Austin). The intensive form of the verb "to write" (occurring only here) suggests these leaders "constantly" or "repeatedly" wrote oppressive rulings (Cambridge Bible). Ellicott notes that "all the formalities of justice were observed punctiliously" — the decisions were duly written and recorded — but the outcome was that the poor, the widow, and the orphan got no redress.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/10-1.htm (Ellicott, Gill, Barnes, Cambridge, K&D), https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_10_commentary

**v. 2: "…to deprive the poor of fair treatment…to make widows their prey and orphans their plunder."**

The specific victims are the *needy* (Hebrew *dal* — the low, helpless, those of humble rank), the *poor* (*ani* — afflicted, dependent), widows, and orphans. These four classes were specially protected in God's Law (Ex 22:22; Dt 24:17–18). The irony is that the very ones YHWH commanded to protect are made "spoil and plunder" (Utley, cited at Precept Austin). Barnes notes that judges "by their office are particularly bound to preserve their rights; and it therefore evinces peculiar iniquity when they who should be their protectors become, in fact, their oppressors." The words for "prey" and "plunder" are the same as those found in the name *Maher-Shalal-Hash-Baz* (Isaiah 8:1), suggesting the principle that men reap what they sow (Ellicott).

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/10-1.htm, https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_10_commentary

**v. 3: "What will you do on the day of reckoning when devastation comes from afar? To whom will you flee for help? Where will you leave your wealth?"**

Three rhetorical questions, each expecting a negative answer: no escape, no helper, no safe place for wealth. The "day of visitation" (KJV) is when God arrives to execute justice (Pulpit Commentary). The "devastation from afar" is the Assyrian army — notoriously brutal. Precept Austin cites Wikipedia and Boyd on Assyrian atrocities: flaying, impaling, burning captives alive. "Corrupt wealth buys helplessness" (ESV Study Bible, cited at Precept Austin). There is a tragic irony: the only true refuge is the very God who is bringing the devastation through Assyria.

- **URLs:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_10_commentary

**v. 4: "Nothing will remain but to crouch among the captives or fall among the slain. Despite all this, His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised."**

The Hebrew verb *kara* (crouch/bow) never means worship — unlike *shachah*. Since the leaders refused to bow in worship before Jehovah, they would be forced to bow before pagan invaders in humiliation (Precept Austin). The final refrain ("His anger is not turned away; His hand is still upraised") is the fourth and last occurrence of this line (see Isa 9:12, 17, 21), marking the conclusion of the oracle against the Northern Kingdom (Precept Austin). Keil & Delitzsch note that the verb *kara* is singular — "used contemptuously, embracing all the high persons as one condensed mass."

- **URLs:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_10_commentary, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/10-1.htm

---

## Verses 5–19: Assyria — God's Instrument, Then Judged

**v. 5: "Woe to Assyria, the rod of My anger; the staff in their hands is My wrath."**

A new section begins, the "burden of Assyria." The "woe" (*hoi*) pronounced on Israel now becomes a "woe" on Assyria. Assyria is called God's "rod" and "staff" — shepherd's instruments of correction. The key theological point: God uses a wicked nation as His instrument of judgment, yet holds that nation accountable for its own wicked motives. Ellicott says this was likely directed at Sargon (who reigned 721–705 BC) or Sennacherib (704–681 BC). The Hebrew of "staff in their hands" is difficult; Cambridge Bible calls it "an absolutely refractory clause" and suggests omitting "it is in their hand" as a gloss, rendering simply "and the staff of mine indignation." Matthew Henry: "The tyrants of the world are tools of Providence."

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/10-5.htm (Ellicott, Barnes, Matthew Henry, JFB, Cambridge, Poole, Gill, K&D), https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

**v. 6: "I will send him against a godless nation…"**

Assyria is "on a mission from God" yet unwittingly so. God gives them charge to "seize spoils" and "trample them down like clay in the streets." The "godless nation" is primarily Israel/Judah — God's own people who had become godless. Guzik (Enduring Word) notes the theological tension: Assyria does God's will but does not intend to; they are held accountable for their own evil intentions while God sovereignly uses their actions.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/10-5.htm

**v. 7: "But this is not his intention; this is not his plan. For it is in his heart to destroy and cut off many nations."**

The distinction between God's purpose (chastisement) and Assyria's purpose (annihilation and conquest) is emphasized. Assyria did not care about God's will or glory — they simply wanted to "destroy and cut off many nations" (Guzik). This is a key biblical principle: God can use the wickedness of man to further His will without ever approving of that wickedness. Guzik cites Psalm 76:10 ("Surely the wrath of man shall praise You") and gives examples of Joseph's brothers, Saul, and Judas.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

**v. 8: "Are not all my commanders kings?"**

The arrogance of Assyria: they considered their princes on a level with the kings of other nations (Guzik). This begins the boast of the Assyrian king, quoted by the prophet.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

**v. 9: "Is not Calno like Carchemish? Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus?"**

A list of conquered cities that fell to Assyria between 740 and 721 BC (Wolf, cited in Guzik). The boast: "Just as all these fell, so will Jerusalem." Carchemish was the latest conquest (717 BC), which helps date the prophecy (Cambridge Bible). Dummelow notes the cities were captured between 740 and 717 BC, so the boast must be later than 717.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/isaiah-10.html

**v. 10–11: "As my hand seized the idolatrous kingdoms…will I not also do to Jerusalem and her idols?"**

Assyria viewed the God of Israel as just another local deity — no different from the idols of conquered nations. This was their fatal theological error. Wolf (cited in Guzik): "none of the gods of these areas had provided the slightest help. It was assumed that the 'idols' (v.10) of Jerusalem were equally impotent." The irony is that Jerusalem *did* have idols (as the Assyrian assumed), which was itself a cause for God's judgment. Matthew Henry laments that Jerusalem "should have set up graven images" and that it was sad the heathen "excelled them in" such things.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/, https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/10-5.htm

**v. 12: "So when the Lord has completed all His work against Mount Zion and Jerusalem, He will say, 'I will punish the king of Assyria for the fruit of his arrogant heart and the proud look in his eyes.'"**

God first finishes His disciplinary work on Zion, then turns to judge the instrument. The "proud look" (*haughty looks*) is specifically condemned in Proverbs 21:4, Psalm 101:5, and Psalm 18:27 — all cited by Guzik. This verse is the hinge of the chapter: God's sovereignty over both the chastisement and the chastiser.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

**v. 13–14: "By the strength of my hand I have done this…I have gathered all the earth…"**

The Assyrian king's boast revels in his own strength (*"by the strength of my hand"*), wisdom (*"by my wisdom, for I am clever"*), and effortless conquest (*"like one gathering abandoned eggs"*). Guzik compares this to Julius Caesar's *"Veni, vidi, vici"* and contrasts it with Charles V's better attitude: *"Veni, vidi, sed Christus vicit"* ("I came, I saw, but Christ conquered"). He claims no resistance: "no wing fluttered, no beak opened or chirped" — a picture of utter helplessness before Assyrian might.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

**v. 15: "Does an axe raise itself above the one who swings it? Does a saw boast over him who saws with it?"**

God's assessment of Assyrian arrogance using the images of an axe, saw, rod, and staff. The instrument cannot claim credit for what the worker does with it. Guzik: "The scalpel can't take credit for what the surgeon does; the strength and the skill are in the user, not in the instrument." This applies to willing instruments of God too — Jesus taught, "We are unprofitable servants" (Luke 17:10).

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

**v. 16–17: "Therefore the Lord GOD of Hosts will send a wasting disease among Assyria's stout warriors… the Light of Israel will become a fire…"**

God's judgment on Assyria is pictured as a wasting disease (*leanness*) and a consuming fire. "The Light of Israel" and "its Holy One" (titles for God) will become a fire that burns Assyria's "thorns and thistles" — the proud warriors and pomp of the empire — "in a single day." This points to the suddenness of the destruction.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

**v. 18–19: "The splendor of its forests and orchards, both soul and body, it will completely destroy… The remaining trees…so few that a child could count them."**

The metaphor shifts to a forest consumed. "Both soul and body" indicates total destruction. Guzik cites Bultema on Calvin's warning: this does not mean the soul is not immortal; rather, "the soul of this tyrant will have to pay for his wicked deeds on earth after the destruction of His body." The remnant of Assyria's army will be so small "a child could count them" (Poole: "a child may be their muster-master").

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

---

## Verses 20–27: The Remnant of Israel and Comfort for Zion

**v. 20: "On that day the remnant of Israel…will no longer depend on him who struck them, but they will truly rely on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel."**

"In that day" points to a future time after God's judgment. The remnant will learn the lesson that Ahaz refused to learn — they will stop trusting in foreign alliances (specifically Assyria, "him who struck them") and will "truly rely on the LORD." This is the fulfillment of the name *Shear-jashub* ("a remnant shall return," Isaiah 7:3). Guzik notes the "remarkable grace and longsuffering of God": even in the midst of deserved judgment, God comforts His people.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

**v. 21: "A remnant will return — a remnant of Jacob — to the Mighty God."**

"A remnant will return" is literally the meaning of *Shear-jashub*, Isaiah's son's name (Isaiah 7:3). "Mighty God" (*El Gibbor*) is the same title used of the Messiah in Isaiah 9:6. Poole sees this as pointing to the Messiah explicitly: "the remnant shall return…unto the mighty God; unto the Messiah, expressly called the mighty God, Isaiah 9:6." This is a key Messianic connection.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/10.htm (quoted in earlier search results)

**v. 22–23: "Though your people, O Israel, be like the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return…"**

Paul quotes these verses in Romans 9:27–28 to explain that not all ethnic Israel is true, believing Israel. The Abrahamic promise of descendants "like the sand of the sea" (Gen 22:17) is not negated but qualified: only a remnant will be saved. "Destruction has been decreed, overflowing with righteousness" — the judgment is both certain and just (Cambridge Bible: "extermination is decreed overflowing in righteousness"). The "determined end" (or "consumption decreed") that God will carry out is a judgment that reduces the teeming population to a remnant.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/isaiah/10.htm, https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

**v. 24: "Therefore this is what the Lord GOD of Hosts says: 'O My people who dwell in Zion, do not fear Assyria…'"**

A direct word of comfort to Jerusalem. "Do not fear" — even though judgment and correction are coming and will hurt, God has a plan. The Assyrians are "striking with a rod" and "lifting his staff" as the Egyptians did (referring to the Egyptian oppression before the Exodus). Guzik: "Because the Assyrians are not in charge, the LORD is."

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

**v. 25: "For in just a little while My fury against you will subside, and My anger will turn to their destruction."**

God's anger against His people is temporary and measured; His anger against Assyria will be destructive. The "little while" indicates that the chastisement, though painful, has a definite endpoint.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

**v. 26: "And the LORD of Hosts will brandish a whip against them, as when He struck Midian at the rock of Oreb. He will raise His staff over the sea, as He did in Egypt."**

Two historical allusions: (1) Gideon's victory over Midian at the rock of Oreb (Judges 7:25) — a miraculous, complete victory; (2) the parting of the Red Sea with Moses' rod (Exodus 14:16) — divine intervention against a seemingly unstoppable enemy. Guzik notes that 2 Kings 19:35 records the fulfillment: "the angel of the LORD…killed 185,000 Assyrians in one night."

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

**v. 27: "On that day the burden will be lifted from your shoulders, and the yoke from your neck. The yoke will be broken because your neck will be too large."**

**This verse contains a significant translation difference.** The BSB reads "because your neck will be too large" (following some Hebrew manuscripts), while the KJV/NKJV read "because of the anointing oil." The Hebrew can be read as *shamen* ("fat/ stout") or *shemen* ("oil/anointing"). 

- **Traditional KJV reading ("because of the anointing"):** Guzik (who preaches from the NKJV) sees the "anointing oil" as representative of the Holy Spirit's presence and power, by which the yoke of bondage is destroyed. He also notes Bultema's view that "the Anointed One" (Messiah) is in view — Jesus is the source of victory and freedom.
- **Modern translation reading ("too large/fat"):** The idea is that the neck grows so fat/strong that the yoke simply breaks — a vivid picture of growth into freedom.

The Pulpit Commentary (cited at StudyLight) takes the traditional reading and applies it devotionally: the yoke is destroyed "because of the grand anointing of our Lord Jesus Christ by God Himself" and "because of the anointing which we have received of Him." This is a good example of how translation differences affect interpretation.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

---

## Verses 28–34: Assyria's March and Sudden Fall

**vv. 28–31: "Assyria has entered Aiath and passed through Migron…"**

A vivid, almost cinematic description of the Assyrian army's advance from north to south. The cities listed trace a route from Aiath (Ai) in the north, through Migron, Michmash (where they store supplies), across the pass to Geba (where they lodge), past Ramah and Gibeah of Saul (both terrified), to Gallim, Laishah, Anathoth, Madmenah, and Gebim — all in panic and flight. Guzik calls this "a deft poetic touch" (Wolf) showing the enemy moving "through twelve different locations, coming ever closer to the capital." 

Dummelow notes that this route is "the usual route from the N" and may be an "ideal description" rather than Sennacherib's actual route (which historically came from the Philistine plain). The prophecy was given before the event, and Isaiah pictures the natural approach route.

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/isaiah-10.html

**v. 32: "Yet today they will halt at Nob, shaking a fist at the mount of Daughter Zion, at the hill of Jerusalem."**

Nob is right on the outskirts of Jerusalem — within sight of the city. This is as far as the Assyrians got. They shake their fist in defiance at Mount Zion but advance no further. Historically, 2 Kings 19:35 records that 185,000 Assyrians were killed by the angel of the LORD in one night, and the army withdrew. Guzik: "They were stopped here."

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

**vv. 33–34: "Behold, the Lord GOD of Hosts will lop off the branches with terrifying power… Lebanon will fall before the Mighty One."**

The metaphor returns to the forest imagery from vv. 18–19. "Those of high stature will be hewn down, and the haughty will be humbled." God is the woodsman wielding the axe. "Lebanon" represents the mighty cedars — the proud, seemingly invincible Assyrian army. "Lebanon will fall by the Mighty One" — the same title (*El Gibbor*) used in v. 21 and Isaiah 9:6 for the Messiah. Guzik: "The bigger they are, the harder they fall down."

- **URLs:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-10/

## Denominational Perspectives

Due to search limitations, I could not retrieve dedicated pages from each denominational tradition. However, from the material gathered, several distinct emphases emerge:

**Reformed/Presbyterian:** This chapter is central to the Reformed understanding of divine sovereignty over human history. Keil & Delitzsch (a standard Reformed-leaning conservative commentary) emphasizes God's absolute control: "Asshur, after having served for a time as the goad of Jehovah's wrath, now falls a victim to that wrath itself." The remnant theology in vv. 20–23 is foundational to the Reformed doctrine of election — Paul's use of this passage in Romans 9:27–28 is key.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik):** Guzik, from a Calvary Chapel (broadly charismatic-evangelical) tradition, emphasizes the Holy Spirit's role in v. 27 ("the anointing oil" as the Spirit's power to break bondage) and sees a Messianic/christological reading throughout. The emphasis is on personal application: God can use evil done to you for good, and the believer should trust God even when correction hurts.

**Methodist/Wesleyan:** Matthew Henry (used across traditions, but beloved in Wesleyan circles) emphasizes the moral dimension: hypocritical religion must be corrected, and affliction is meant "to bring sin to their remembrance, and humble them, and to awaken them to a sense of their duty."

**Dispensational (Precept Austin references):** Precept Austin explicitly warns readers that some commentaries "have jettisoned a literal approach to the interpretation of Scripture and have 'replaced' Israel with the Church." The dispensational reading sees the remnant promises as applying to literal, ethnic Israel, with the ultimate fulfillment in a future millennial kingdom (Isaiah 11–12).

**Lutheran:** While no Lutheran-specific source was retrieved, the law-gospel dynamic is present: the law (vv. 1–4, 5–19) condemns unjust rulers and arrogant empires; the gospel (vv. 20–27) promises deliverance through God's gracious intervention, not human merit.

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges):** Raises questions about authorship and date. Notes that "the grounds on which this has been disputed by recent writers (see Cheyne, Introduction, pp. xlviii ff.) are not convincing." Suggests the oracle was written between 717 and 701 BC. Observes that the route described in vv. 28–32 is an "ideal description" — the natural northern approach — not necessarily Sennacherib's actual route from the Philistine plain. Notes the "absolutely refractory" Hebrew clause in v. 5.

- **URLs:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/10-5.htm (Cambridge section), https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/10.htm

**Catholic and Orthodox views:** Search limits prevented retrieval from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org. However, the Catholic Haydock commentary is listed on BibleHub, though its content was not fetched. Generally, Catholic interpretation reads this chapter in continuity with the Church Fathers, seeing Assyria as a type of all proud worldly powers that oppose God's kingdom, and the remnant as prefiguring the Church.

**Translation issue on v. 27:** As noted above, the BSB follows the reading *"your neck will be too large"* (from Hebrew *shamen* = fat/stout), while KJV/NKJV reads *"because of the anointing"* (from *shemen* = oil). This is a classic textual variant where the consonantal text is the same but vocalization differs. The NET Bible notes (available via netbible.org but not fetched due to limits) generally prefer the "fat/grown strong" reading as the more literal rendering.
